title: Forest Friends
missionLabel: Help Mira the Explorer understand the story clues.
passageText: Mira packed a sandwich, a notebook, and a pencil before walking up Pine Hill. The morning air smelled like pine needles and wet soil. At the top, she heard chirping near an old oak tree. Two small birds were carrying tiny twigs to the same branch. Mira sat quietly so she would not scare them away. She noticed that one bird arranged the twigs while the other searched for more. A gust of wind knocked one twig to the ground. Instead of flying away, the bird dropped down, picked it up, and returned to the nest. Mira wrote that teamwork and patience were helping the birds finish a hard job. Before she left, she checked the branch one last time and saw the nest taking shape.

questions.correctChoice: The birds show teamwork while building a nest.
choices: Mira forgot her lunch on Pine Hill.
The birds show teamwork while building a nest.

Mira wants to be a bird scientist someday.

questions.prompt: Write 2-3 sentences explaining one clue that shows the birds did not give up.

title: How Bees Help Flowers
missionLabel: Read the facts and discover why pollinators matter.
passageText: Bees visit flowers to collect nectar and pollen during warm parts of the day. As they crawl inside blooms, pollen sticks to tiny hairs on their legs and bodies. When bees travel to the next flower, some of that pollen rubs off. This transfer process is called pollination. Pollination helps plants produce seeds and fruit. Farmers depend on pollination for crops like berries, melons, and apples. Gardeners also notice stronger harvests when pollinators are active. Bees are not the only pollinators, but they are among the most efficient. Without them, many flowering plants would produce less food. Protecting pollinator habitats helps both wild ecosystems and human communities.

questions.correctChoice: Bees spread pollen from one flower to another.
choices: Bees build hives in flower gardens.
Bees spread pollen from one flower to another.
Flowers make nectar only at night.
Farmers plant fruit trees in rows.

questions.prompt: Summarize why bees are important using two complete sentences.

title: The River Map Clue
missionLabel: Follow clues and infer what happens next.
passageText: Jalen found a folded map under a smooth river rock by the trail. A note on top said to start where the willow tree leaned over the bank. He called his cousin Nia and showed her the drawing. Together they followed the arrows and counted ten steps east. The first spot was empty, so they checked the map again for a second clue. Nia noticed a tiny bird symbol next to a bench on the page. They walked there and found a wooden box under the seat. Inside was a bag of bird seed and a thank-you message from a park volunteer. The note explained that the map was a kindness challenge, not a treasure hunt. Jalen laughed and said the best prize was helping something alive.

questions.correctChoice: They wanted someone to help birds in the park.
choices: They wanted someone to help birds in the park.
They forgot where they hid money.
They planned to close the park.
They wanted Jalen to stay home.

questions.prompt: In 2-3 complete sentences, explain how the ending changes Jalen's idea about the map.

title: Garden Helpers
missionLabel: Discover how living things keep a garden healthy.
passageText: A school garden near the playground grows tomatoes, beans, lettuce, and marigolds. Students check the beds every morning before class starts. They often see worms turning the soil after rainy nights. Those tunnels let water and air reach plant roots more easily. Ladybugs crawl across leaves and eat pests that damage stems. Bees visit blossoms and carry pollen from one flower to another. Compost made from cafeteria scraps adds nutrients to the soil. Students record which beds look healthiest each week. Their chart shows that gardens do best when many helpers work together. The project teaches that healthy systems depend on many small jobs, not one single fix.

questions.correctChoice: Different garden helpers do different jobs to help plants grow.

Tomatoes need less care than other plants.

title: The Mountain Stream
missionLabel: Use clues to infer why a stream changes.
passageText: Kai visited the trail the morning after a long rainstorm ended. The stream that was usually clear looked brown and rushed past the rocks. Small branches floated by in fast swirls. Mud covered the edges of the path near the bridge. Kai saw deep footprints where hikers had stepped around puddles. A wooden trail sign leaned sideways, and one corner was cracked. He remembered that the hill above the stream had loose soil. Heavy rain likely washed that soil downhill into the water. He also guessed that the strong current bumped debris against the signpost. Kai took photos to share with the ranger so repairs could happen quickly.

questions.correctChoice: The stream moved quickly and carried dirt and branches.
choices: Kai walked on the same trail last month.
The bridge was painted green.

title: The Park Ranger Note
missionLabel: Read signs and sequence events in a nature walk.
passageText: Before the class hike, Ranger Lee handed each student a safety card. The card listed four steps in a clear order. First, stay on marked paths so plants and nests are not damaged. Next, carry out all trash, including snack wrappers and juice tops. Then, watch animals from a distance instead of trying to touch them. Last, tell an adult right away if someone in the group gets separated. Ranger Lee explained why each step protects both hikers and wildlife. Students practiced the steps before leaving the trailhead. During the hike, they reminded one another when someone drifted off the path. By the end, the group understood that simple routines can prevent bigger problems.

questions.correctChoice: Watch animals from a distance.
choices: Watch animals from a distance.
Leave the marked path.
Start running ahead.
Ignore the safety note.

questions.prompt: Write two sentences summarizing why the steps are listed in order.

title: Moon Garden Message
missionLabel: Follow a space-themed story and find the big idea.
passageText: Lena placed glow sticks around the community garden for night science club. The sticks marked where students should stand safely in the dark. She pointed to the moon and asked everyone to notice the long shadows. Every ten minutes, the shadow lines moved a little across the path. Lena measured each change with a ruler and wrote it in her chart. Her partner checked the time and called out each interval. Another teammate sketched the garden bed to show where shadows started and ended. By the fourth measurement, the class could see a clear pattern. They discussed how moonlight and Earth movement can change what we see. The club ended the night excited that simple tools could produce real scientific evidence.

title: Planet Parade
missionLabel: Learn vocabulary about the solar system.
passageText: Planets travel around the sun on paths called orbits. An orbit is not a straight line but a curved path that repeats. Planets close to the sun complete shorter trips in less time. Planets farther away have larger paths and need more time to circle once. Earth completes one orbit in about 365 days. Mercury finishes an orbit much faster than Earth because it is closer to the sun. Neptune takes many years because it travels a much longer path. Scientists use models and diagrams to compare these distances. They also use observations from telescopes and space missions to verify movement. Understanding orbits helps explain why years are different lengths on different planets.

questions.prompt: Which sentence best defines orbit?
questions.correctChoice: An orbit is a path a planet follows around the sun.
choices: An orbit is a giant storm on a planet.
An orbit is a path a planet follows around the sun.
An orbit is the amount of sunlight in one day.
An orbit is a telescope used by scientists.

questions.prompt: Write two complete sentences describing why some planets take longer to orbit.

title: Satellite Clue
missionLabel: Infer why a school signal changed during weather class.
passageText: During weather club, Amara checked a tablet that displayed live cloud images from a satellite. She and her team used the pictures to compare local clouds with regional patterns. Suddenly, the screen froze and stopped updating. Amara looked outside and noticed dark storm clouds building quickly. Flags near the field were snapping in strong gusts. The teacher explained that severe weather can interfere with signals for short periods. The club switched to paper maps while they waited. Ten minutes later, the storm moved farther east. The tablet refreshed and began showing new images again. Amara recorded the interruption as evidence that weather can affect communication tools.

choices: The tablet battery ran out forever.

title: Rocket Club Rules
missionLabel: Sequence steps for a safe rocket launch.
passageText: The rocket club follows a strict checklist each time it launches. First, students check that the launch field is clear of people and backpacks. They also confirm that wind conditions are safe for a straight flight. Next, everyone stands behind the painted safety line. One student leads a loud countdown while another watches the rocket angle. Then, the launch switch is pressed only after the teacher gives approval. The rocket rises quickly, and students track it with their eyes. After touchdown, the team waits for an all-clear signal before moving forward. Finally, they inspect the rocket and write notes about the flight. This sequence keeps launch day exciting and safe at the same time.

title: Star Map Helpers
missionLabel: Summarize how a team uses a map of stars.
passageText: Students at Sky Club used a printed star map to find the North Star. They met after sunset in the school field when the sky was clear. One student held a red flashlight so eyes could stay adjusted to darkness. Another student lined up the map with the horizon using a compass. Two teammates searched for the Big Dipper pattern first. From that pattern, they traced an imaginary line toward the North Star. Each student took a turn checking the location to confirm the result. The group marked the position in their notebooks and compared answers. Their notes matched, showing they had found the correct star. Teamwork and careful roles helped the class finish quickly and accurately.

title: Library Day
missionLabel: Use clues to understand how helpers support a community.
passageText: When boxes of new books arrived, Ms. Patel asked the class for help. Marco sorted adventure, science, and history titles into separate stacks. Ana placed new labels on shelves so books could be returned correctly. Two students checked each title against the library list. Another group made bright signs for the reading corner and biography wall. By lunch, the room looked organized but still needed final checks. Ms. Patel asked everyone to test the shelves by finding one book in each category. Students discovered two mislabeled bins and fixed them quickly. In the afternoon, younger classes visited and found books without long waits. The team learned that organized systems make shared spaces easier for everyone.

title: Mail Route Morning
missionLabel: Learn sequence from a community helper's routine.
passageText: A mail carrier starts early at the post office each morning. First, letters and small packages are sorted by neighborhood and street. Next, the carrier places items in route order to save time on the road. A scanner is checked to track deliveries accurately. Then, the carrier drives the route and delivers mail house by house. At each stop, the carrier verifies address numbers before leaving items. If no one is home for a package, a pickup notice is left. By afternoon, undelivered items return to the post office. The route report is updated so families can track important deliveries. This dependable sequence helps the whole community receive mail on time.

title: Bus Stop Safety
missionLabel: Identify the main idea in safety directions.
passageText: Bus safety begins before the bus even arrives. Students should stand back from the curb while they wait. Backpacks should stay zipped so straps do not catch on rails. Pushing or rough play can cause accidents in crowded lines. When the bus stops, students form one line and wait for the driver's signal. Boarding one at a time keeps steps clear and reduces confusion. Once seated, students keep aisles open for others to move safely. The same calm behavior is important when leaving the bus after school. Drivers rely on these routines to protect every rider. Following simple rules makes the trip safer and smoother for everyone.

title: Clinic Visit

title: Recycling Team

passageText: The school recycling team meets every Tuesday after lunch. They start by checking labels on paper, plastic, and metal bins. title: Soccer Formation

passageText: At halftime, Coach Ruiz moved Maya from defense to midfield. Maya felt surprised but listened carefully to the new plan. title: Relay Race Steps
missionLabel: Follow sequence directions for a relay exchange.
passageText: In a relay race, each runner has a marked exchange zone. Before practice, Coach Allen draws the zone lines in bright chalk. First, the waiting runner starts jogging when the teammate reaches the signal cone. Next, the waiting runner reaches a hand back without turning around. The incoming runner calls "stick" so the teammate knows the pass is coming. Then, the baton is placed firmly into the open hand. If the pass is shaky, both runners slow down and try the exchange again. Last, the new runner drives forward and builds speed down the lane. Teams practice this sequence many times to make it smooth and safe. A clean exchange can save valuable seconds in a close race.

title: Swim Practice Focus

passageText: Coach Kim planned short swim sets with rest breaks for the first week of training. She explained that endurance means keeping your body moving for a long time without losing control. Coach Kim used the chart to show progress over several days. In week two, she increased the number of laps in each set. The team noticed they could keep pace longer before feeling tired. By Friday, most swimmers completed the new sets without stopping. They learned that endurance grows through steady practice, not fast starts.

title: Gym Fair Play
missionLabel: Summarize rules that support respectful play.
passageText: In gym class games, students follow fair-play rules from the first whistle to the last. Teams shake hands before each game to show respect. If a foul happens, players call it honestly instead of arguing. Referee decisions are accepted so the game can continue safely. Coaches remind students to encourage teammates after mistakes. Positive words help players reset and focus on the next play. At halftime, teams check whether everyone feels included. After the game, players shake hands again and thank opponents. These habits keep competition friendly, even when the score is close. Fair play makes sports more fun and safer for everyone involved.

title: Paper Bridge Challenge

questions.prompt: How did Nia's actions affect Omar?
questions.correctChoice: Her support helped him become more confident with the routine.
choices: Her support helped him become more confident with the routine.
He stopped eating lunch.
He asked to leave school.
He forgot how to carry a tray.

questions.prompt: Write two complete sentences explaining which details show Omar's confidence improved.
